prompt.context_jp: テーブルに広げられた温泉宿のパンフレットに視線___集まり、日ごろの緊張が少しずつほぐれていく。
prompt.prompt_jp: テーブルに広げられた温泉宿のパンフレットに視線___集まり…

feedback.correct_en: が marks the new scene element — 'gazes gather' is a fresh observation at the start of the izakaya scene, not a continuing topic.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would signal 視線 as an already-established topic, which doesn't fit this descriptive opening. を is wrong because 集まる is intransitive.

contrast_examples.en: Gazes gather (new event).

contrast_examples.jp: 視線は彼女に向いていた。
contrast_examples.en: The gazes (topic) were on her.

prompt.prompt_jp: 私も今の課長___最悪だから ひと晩中 しゃべれるかも

feedback.correct_en: は presents 課長 as the topic she's complaining about — 'as for my current manager, he's the worst.' It fits the complaint-sharing register.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would mark it as newly identified info ('it is the manager who is the worst'), but here she's just launching into a topic.

contrast_examples.en: My current manager is the worst (topic).

contrast_examples.jp: 最悪なのは今の課長だ。
contrast_examples.en: The one who's the worst is my current manager (focus).

prompt.prompt_jp: ねえ なんか 舞___さ おっさんっぽくなったよね

feedback.correct_en: 舞は marks Mai as the topic of the comment ('as for Mai, she's gotten...'). The casual さ emphasizes topic-marking in conversation.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make it sound like identifying who became old-mannish out of a set, but the friends are just commenting on Mai directly.

contrast_examples.en: Mai is like an old man (topic).
It's Mai who's like an old man (identifying).

prompt.prompt_jp: デスクに広げられた週刊誌の見出し___、行員たちの視線を釘付けにしていたのである。

feedback.correct_en: が introduces 見出し as the new scene element being described — a narrative descriptive clause explaining what grabbed attention.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make the headline an already-known topic, but the narrator is presenting it freshly as the cause of the commotion.

contrast_examples.jp: 見出しが視線を釘付けにしていた。
contrast_examples.en: The headline was riveting attention (new element).

contrast_examples.jp: その見出しは衝撃的だった。
contrast_examples.en: That headline (topic) was shocking.

prompt.prompt_jp: 週刊誌を握りしめた芝崎次長___、息を切らして臨店班のフロアへ駆け込んできたのである。

feedback.correct_en: が marks Shibazaki as a new participant bursting into the scene — classic new-information が in narrative description.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat Shibazaki as an established topic, but he's being introduced into this scene for the first time.

contrast_examples.jp: 芝崎次長が駆け込んできた。
contrast_examples.en: Shibazaki came rushing in (new on scene).

contrast_examples.jp: 芝崎次長はいつもそうだ。
contrast_examples.en: Shibazaki (topic) is always like that.

prompt.prompt_jp: 「“メガバンク Ｔ銀行”って この写真___ あからさまに ウチじゃないですか？」

feedback.correct_en: は presents この写真 as the topic they're examining ('as for this photo, isn't it obviously ours?').
feedback.incorrect_en: が would sound like identifying which photo it is out of several, but they're commenting on one specific photo already in view.

contrast_examples.jp: この写真はウチの銀行だ。
contrast_examples.en: This photo is our bank (topic-comment).

contrast_examples.jp: ウチの銀行なのはこの写真だ。
contrast_examples.en: The one that's our bank is this photo (focus).

prompt.prompt_jp: 「“告発したの___ Ｔ銀行の 都内 某支店の窓口で働く” “20代の現役女子行員”」

feedback.correct_en: は in a nominalized 〜のは…だ structure marks the topic ('the one who exposed it is…'). It presents what follows as the specifying predicate.
feedback.incorrect_en: が here would break the cleft structure 〜のは〜だ, which is the natural frame for identifying a person described by a prior clause.

contrast_examples.en: The one who exposed it is her.
She exposed it (plain).

prompt.prompt_jp: 「ホントにやりそうだな 花咲君___」

feedback.correct_en: は works here with the inverted word order — 花咲君 is the topic the speaker is commenting on ('she really would, that Hanasaki').
feedback.incorrect_en: が would turn it into identification ('it's Hanasaki who seems like she'd do it'), losing the familiar commenting nuance.

contrast_examples.en: Hanasaki (topic) seems like she'd do it.
It was Hanasaki who did it.

prompt.prompt_jp: それでも上司の指示___絶対で、二人は姿勢を正して次の言葉を待った。

feedback.correct_en: は marks 上司の指示 as a topic for a general/characterizing statement ('a boss's orders are absolute'). This is a maxim-like proposition.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make it sound like identifying what's absolute in this specific moment, missing the generalizing tone.

contrast_examples.en: A boss's orders are absolute (general truth).
The boss's orders arrived (event).

prompt.prompt_jp: 「大丈夫です 支店の問題を解決してきた 頼もしいコンビです___」

feedback.correct_en: から gives the reason ('because they're a reliable duo that has solved branch problems'). The sentence ends justifying 大丈夫です.
feedback.incorrect_en: が/は don't close a reason clause here; the context demands a causal connector supporting the preceding 大丈夫です.

contrast_examples.jp: 頼もしいコンビですから、大丈夫です。
contrast_examples.en: They're reliable, so it's fine.

contrast_examples.jp: 頼もしいコンビですが、心配だ。
contrast_examples.en: They're reliable, but I'm worried.

prompt.prompt_jp: 「信用第一の銀行に スキャンダル___禁物ですからね」

feedback.correct_en: は makes スキャンダル a topic for a general statement ('scandal is taboo for a trust-first bank'). It states a principle.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would focus on what specifically is forbidden, losing the general-truth framing appropriate to the context.

contrast_examples.jp: スキャンダルは禁物だ。
contrast_examples.en: Scandal is to be avoided (principle).

contrast_examples.jp: スキャンダルが起きた。
contrast_examples.en: A scandal happened (event).

prompt.context_jp: 奈津子が試験で落ちたことに
prompt.prompt_jp: 「私 いまだに納得できないんだよね 奈津子___試験で落とされるのなんて」

feedback.correct_en: が marks the subject inside a nominalized clause (奈津子が試験で落とされるの). Embedded subject clauses normally take が, not は.
feedback.incorrect_en: は can't appear as the subject of a subordinate clause nominalized by の — it would try to make 奈津子 the main topic of the whole sentence.

contrast_examples.jp: 奈津子が落ちるなんて信じられない。
contrast_examples.en: I can't believe Natsuko failed (embedded subject).

contrast_examples.jp: 奈津子は試験に落ちた。
contrast_examples.en: Natsuko (topic) failed the exam.

prompt.prompt_jp: と口走った舞の一言___、これから相馬をひどく振り回すことになりそうだった。

feedback.correct_en: が marks 舞の一言 as the newly introduced subject the narrator wants to foreground as the cause of future trouble — descriptive narration.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame it as an already-known topic, but the sentence is spotlighting this specific remark as a fresh plot element.

contrast_examples.jp: 舞の一言が相馬を振り回す。
contrast_examples.en: Mai's remark will throw Souma around (new focus).

contrast_examples.jp: 舞の一言はいつも軽い。
contrast_examples.en: Mai's remarks (topic) are always flippant.

prompt.prompt_jp: 「自分の勤めてる会社を 雑誌に売るなんて よっぽどの覚悟___なきゃ できやしないだろう？」

feedback.correct_en: が is the subject of ある (〜がなきゃ = がなければ). Existence/possession predicates take が for the thing possessed.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would clash with the conditional ない form here; 覚悟はなきゃ sounds ungrammatical in this fixed existence pattern.

contrast_examples.jp: 覚悟がなきゃできない。
contrast_examples.en: You can't without resolve.
I have resolve (contrastive/topic).

prompt.prompt_jp: 「Ａ子さんって きっと」「責任感___強くて 真面目な人なんですよ」

feedback.correct_en: が appears in the 〜は〜が〜 double-subject pattern: A子さんは (topic) + 責任感が強い (attribute). The attribute's subject takes が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would create two competing topics in one clause, which isn't how attribute-description works. 責任感 is the attribute of the topic.

contrast_examples.en: She has a strong sense of responsibility.
She is tall (same pattern).

prompt.prompt_jp: 「私だよ このメール出したの___ 私」

feedback.correct_en: は in the cleft 〜のは〜 marks the topic ('as for the one who sent the email, it's me'). It identifies Natsuko as the sender.
feedback.incorrect_en: が wouldn't fit this cleft frame — the pattern for revealing identity after a nominalized clause is 〜のは〜だ.

contrast_examples.jp: このメールを出したのは私だ。
contrast_examples.en: The one who sent this email is me.

contrast_examples.jp: 私がこのメールを出した。
contrast_examples.en: I sent this email (plain).

prompt.prompt_jp: 「でも 支店の人事評価をつけるの___ 支店長だから」

feedback.correct_en: は in the cleft structure 〜のは〜だ identifies who is responsible ('the one who assigns evaluations is the branch manager').
feedback.incorrect_en: が would double up the subject role and break the clean cleft presentation of this identifying statement.

contrast_examples.en: The one who decides is the manager.
The manager decides.

prompt.prompt_jp: 「彼女が何を言っても 証拠___ない以上 大前は認めないだろう」

feedback.correct_en: が is the subject of the existence predicate ない within a subordinate 以上-clause. Existence predicates and embedded clauses favor が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would try to make 証拠 the main topic, but it's inside a subordinate 'as long as there's no evidence' clause.

contrast_examples.jp: 証拠がない以上、認めない。
contrast_examples.en: As long as there's no evidence, he won't admit it.
There IS evidence (contrastive).

prompt.prompt_jp: 「舞___すごいね 本部に抜擢されて」

feedback.correct_en: は presents 舞 as the topic the speaker is complimenting ('as for Mai, she's amazing'). Personal evaluation takes topic は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would sound like identifying which of them is amazing — out of place when directly addressing a friend about her.

contrast_examples.en: Mai is amazing (topic).
The amazing one is Mai (focus).

prompt.prompt_jp: 翌朝の東京第一銀行のオフィスは、いつもとは違うざわめきに___ていた。

feedback.correct_en: ざわめきに包まれる is the natural collocation for an atmosphere/mood enveloping a space.
feedback.incorrect_en: 覆われる implies physical covering (snow, cloth); 満たされる is used with emotions/liquids filling a space, not with ざわめき.

contrast_examples.jp: 店内は笑い声に包まれた。
contrast_examples.en: The shop was wrapped in laughter.
The mountain is covered in snow.

prompt.prompt_jp: 「公私混同 ___です！ こんなことされたら 殴っちゃうかも…」

feedback.correct_en: 言語道断 ('outrageous/unspeakable') fits Mai's indignation at mixing personal and professional conduct.
feedback.incorrect_en: 一石二鳥 means 'two birds with one stone'; 自業自得 means 'reap what you sow'. Neither expresses outrage.

contrast_examples.jp: そんな行為は言語道断だ。
contrast_examples.en: Such behavior is utterly unacceptable.
This is two birds with one stone.

prompt.prompt_jp: 都内数千人の女子行員の中からたった一人を探し出せというのは、まさに___ような話である。

feedback.correct_en: 雲をつかむような話 is the idiom for 'a vague, hopeless task' — fits searching one person among thousands.
feedback.incorrect_en: 手を焼く means 'to be at a loss handling someone'; 腰を据える means 'to settle in to do something properly'. Neither fits here.

contrast_examples.jp: 雲をつかむような話だ。
contrast_examples.en: It's like trying to grasp a cloud.
To have trouble handling a child.

prompt.prompt_jp: 「…面白おかしく書かれるのが ___だよ」

feedback.correct_en: 関の山 means 'the best one can hope for / the most that will happen' — Souma says being mocked is the most we'd achieve.
feedback.incorrect_en: 山の神 means 'wife'; 背水の陣 is 'last stand'. Neither expresses a ceiling of possibility.

contrast_examples.jp: 笑われるのが関の山だ。
contrast_examples.en: Being laughed at is the most you can expect.
To make a last stand.

prompt.prompt_jp: 「___です！ 私が 内部告発をして 勤めていた銀行に 迷惑をかけるような人間に 見えますか！？」

feedback.correct_en: 心外 expresses offense at being wrongly suspected — the perfect word for her indignation.
feedback.incorrect_en: 意外 just means 'unexpected' without offense; 例外 means 'exception'. Only 心外 carries the hurt-and-angry nuance.

contrast_examples.en: Being suspected is deeply offensive.
The result was unexpected.

prompt.prompt_jp: 「そう考えると 相当 ___ていたのかなって」

feedback.correct_en: 追い詰められる means 'to be cornered/driven into a corner' — the natural expression for being under extreme pressure.
feedback.incorrect_en: 追いかけられる is 'to be chased'; 追い抜かれる is 'to be overtaken'. Neither captures emotional cornering.

contrast_examples.jp: 精神的に追い詰められる。
contrast_examples.en: To be psychologically cornered.
To be chased by a dog.

prompt.prompt_jp: 「___が切れたみたいに 我慢できなくなっちゃって」

feedback.correct_en: 糸が切れる is the standard metaphor for emotional restraint snapping — a thread of self-control breaking.
feedback.incorrect_en: 縁が切れる means 'to sever ties'; 気が切れる isn't a standard idiom. Only 糸 captures the sudden emotional snap.

contrast_examples.en: The thread of tension snapped.
My ties with him were severed.

prompt.prompt_jp: 「___正論は 時に ジャマになるからな」

feedback.correct_en: 薄っぺらい正論 = 'shallow/superficial platitudes' — Shindo dismisses rigid justice as thin reasoning.
feedback.incorrect_en: 分厚い describes physical thickness; 甘ったるい means 'sickly sweet'. Neither pairs with 正論 to mean 'shallow argument'.

contrast_examples.en: A shallow argument.
A thick book.

prompt.context_jp: 奈津子が告白する場面
prompt.prompt_jp: どちらが自然ですか？
prompt.prompt_en: Which sounds more natural in Natsuko's confession?

choices.text: 友達だから… 言えなかったの
友達なので… 言えませんでした

feedback.correct_en: The casual 〜だから + 〜なかったの fits two friends having a vulnerable private conversation. Natsuko uses familiar speech with Mai.
feedback.incorrect_en: 〜なので + 〜ませんでした is polite/formal register, which clashes with the intimate close-friend setting.

contrast_examples.jp: 友達だから言えなかった。
contrast_examples.en: Because we're friends, I couldn't say it (casual).

contrast_examples.jp: 友達なので申し上げられませんでした。
contrast_examples.en: Because we are friends, I could not say it (formal).

prompt.prompt_jp: 舞らしい決意表明として自然なのは？
prompt.prompt_en: Which fits Mai's impulsive personality better?

choices.text: 見つけられるよう努力いたします

feedback.correct_en: 絶対見つけます matches Mai's blunt, impulsive 'つい' style that even Souma criticizes afterward. It's the line that drives the plot.
feedback.incorrect_en: 努力いたします is cautious corporate hedging — exactly what Souma wishes Mai would say instead.

contrast_examples.en: I'll definitely do it!
I will endeavor to do so.

prompt.context_jp: 舞が大前次長に意見する
prompt.prompt_jp: 上司に遠慮しつつ意見する場面として自然なのは？
prompt.prompt_en: Which is more natural when hesitantly challenging a superior?

choices.text: ずっと 気になってたんですけど…なんか おかしくないですか？
ずっと気になってた。おかしいよね？

feedback.correct_en: The 〜んですけど softener + question form lets Mai push back on a senior while maintaining workplace politeness.
feedback.incorrect_en: The plain-form version is far too casual for addressing 大前次長 and would be shockingly rude.

contrast_examples.jp: 気になってたんですけど、おかしくないですか？
contrast_examples.en: I've been wondering — isn't it strange? (polite pushback)

contrast_examples.jp: 気になってた。おかしいよね？
contrast_examples.en: I was wondering. Isn't it weird? (casual)
